content.rendered:
This free fake Xbox update screen makes a console look like it has been hijacked by a system update at the worst possible moment. It opens on “Preparing console…”, works through Downloading, Verifying and Applying with a percentage that genuinely climbs, holds at 100% — and then goes black and starts the whole thing again. Nothing is downloaded, no console is contacted, and ESC ends it instantly.

What the fake Xbox update screen does

Almost every console-update joke online is a screenshot or a looping video, and neither survives more than a few seconds of real attention. A video loops visibly. A screenshot never moves. A working fake Xbox update has to behave like software rather than like an image, so this one is a live screen: the bar advances, the stage percentage ticks up one number at a time, the overall figure creeps along behind it, and the wording changes as each step completes.

It reproduces the dark “Updating…” layout: left-aligned text against near-black, “Sit tight while we update your Xbox.” underneath, a download arrow on the right of the screen, and three progress segments along the bottom edge. Above them sits the line that does more work than anything else on the page — “Your console will restart during the update.”

Preparing console, then three steps

Starting from zero, the fake Xbox update opens on a preparation screen: a single progress track, no stage label, and “Don’t turn off or unplug your console.” It sits there for a moment the way a real one does before it commits to anything. Then the three-track update screen takes over and works through its steps in order.

  • Downloading. The longest step, and the one that carries most of the overall progress. This is where a real update spends its time, so this is where the fake one spends its time too.
  • Verifying. Brief. It flashes past quickly enough that anyone watching relaxes slightly, right before the longest wait of the cycle begins.
  • Applying. The slow one. It crawls, and because the overall percentage is already high by this point, it is the step that makes people sit down and wait rather than walk away.

Each step shows its own percentage alongside the overall figure, which is the detail most imitations miss. On a real console those two numbers disagree constantly — the step is at 63% while the update as a whole is at 33% — and seeing them disagree is a large part of why this fake Xbox update reads as genuine.

Why the percentage stops moving

A progress bar that slides evenly from 0 to 100 is the single clearest tell that an update is fake, because no real one has ever behaved that way. Console updates crawl, stop dead on one number long enough to make you worry, then jump forward. This screen does the same thing deliberately: it pauses partway through each step before moving on.

Those pauses do most of the persuading. They are the moments when someone leans in, mutters that it has frozen, and then relaxes when it starts moving again — which sets them up perfectly for the step change that follows. A smooth bar gets ignored; a stalled one gets stared at. It is the cheapest realism in the whole fake Xbox update, and it costs nothing but a few seconds of patience.

The update that never finishes

There is no completion state. The screen runs its three steps, holds at 100% just long enough to look like it is about to reboot, then goes black — and comes back on “Preparing console…”, ready to do it all again. No percentage it can reach ends it.

No button ends it either. There is no cancel option, no menu and no detail view anywhere on the screen, because the instant a fake Xbox update offers a way out, the joke is over — someone presses it and the illusion collapses. If you switch on the optional warning before launching, clicks and key presses raise “Don’t turn off your console” instead of doing anything useful. ESC and the invisible top-right exit area always work.

The black restart between cycles is doing quiet work too. An update that simply looped back to zero would eventually look like an animation on repeat. One that completes, blanks the screen, and starts preparing again looks like a console caught in a genuine update loop — which is a thing that really happens, and which every Xbox owner has heard stories about.

How to set it up

A worked example, using the setup that tends to work best. Say someone is about to sit down for an evening of gaming:

  1. Set Starting progress to 73%. The fake Xbox update then opens partway through Applying, as though it is nearly done.
  2. Set Update speed to Slow if you are leaving the room, or Normal if you are standing there watching.
  3. Decide on the warning. Left off, the screen ignores every button press in silence. Switched on, it answers each one with “Don’t turn off your console.”
  4. Press Start Fake Update, then hand over the controller or step away from the screen.

The 73% opening is worth the extra second it takes to set. Starting at zero tells someone they have ten minutes to kill and they will go and do something else. Starting at 73% tells them it is nearly over, so they sit and wait — and then watch it reach the end, go black, and start preparing all over again. Very few people walk away from an update that is apparently three-quarters finished.

Making it look right on a TV

This prank lives or dies on the screen it runs on, more than most. An update screen on a laptop display is obviously a web page; the same screen on the living-room television is genuinely hard to argue with. If you can connect a laptop to the TV over HDMI and switch the input, the illusion is close to complete — the Xbox is sitting right there, the TV is showing its update screen, and nothing about the picture contradicts that.

Launch the prank before you switch inputs so nobody sees a browser. Once it is running, the page is fullscreen and there is no address bar, no tab strip and no cursor unless you move the mouse. Moving the mouse does not reveal an exit badge. Press ESC or click or tap the invisible exit area in the top-right corner when you are finished.

What gives a fake update away

Three things, in order of how often they ruin it. The first is a bar that moves too smoothly, which this page fixes with the pauses described above. The second is wrong wording — borrowing another console’s phrasing is spotted instantly by someone who owns an Xbox, which is why this page uses the Xbox copy rather than a generic progress screen with a swapped background colour.

The third is the exit. A prank that ends the moment someone taps the screen was never really running. Ordinary clicks leave this fake Xbox update running exactly as it was, so there is nothing a suspicious person can press that confirms their suspicion. They are left doing precisely what a real stuck update would leave them doing: staring at it.

What it does not do

Nothing on this page reaches a console. It cannot, and that is worth being plain about, because “update” is a word that makes people nervous. The screen is HTML, CSS and JavaScript running inside a browser tab. The percentage is a number counting up in the page, disconnected from any system anywhere. No file is downloaded, no firmware is touched, no save data or game install is read or changed, no account is signed into, and nothing is installed on any device.

The moment you press ESC, the screen disappears and the browser is exactly as it was. Closing the tab has the same effect. There is no cleanup step and nothing to undo — a fake Xbox update has no way to leave a trace on hardware it never touched in the first place.

When to leave this one alone

It is one of the gentler pranks on the site — nobody believes their console is broken, only that it has chosen the worst possible moment to update, which every player has genuinely lived through. That shared experience is exactly why it works, and also why it is worth a little judgement about timing. Do not run a fake Xbox update on someone about to start a ranked match, a raid with other people waiting, or a session they have been looking forward to all week. The joke is the sinking feeling of a badly timed update, and that feeling stops being funny fast if the match was real.

Can you run it on the Xbox itself?

You can, and it is the most convincing way to do this. Xbox consoles have a web browser available from the store, so you can open this page on the console itself and launch the fake Xbox update there. The screen is then genuinely coming out of the Xbox, on the Xbox’s own display output, with no laptop and no HDMI switching to give the game away.

Two things to watch. Browsing with a controller is slower than a mouse, so set the page up before anyone is in the room rather than fumbling through it in front of them. And know your exit before you start: the controller’s B button and the Xbox guide button both get you out of the browser, which matters because the whole point of this fake Xbox update is that nothing on the screen itself offers a way out.

If the console browser is not installed and you do not want to install it in front of your victim, the laptop-to-HDMI route described above gets you most of the way there. A fake Xbox update on the television reads as real to almost everyone, because nobody checks which input the TV is on when the screen is showing exactly what they expect it to show.

Other console and computer prank screens

Match the prank to the machine. If your target owns a different console, the fake PlayStation update screen uses the blue install screen and its own error code, and the fake Nintendo Switch update screen uses the circular progress ring. For a computer instead, the fake Windows 11 update screen is the direct desktop equivalent, and the fake blue screen of death is the classic if you want alarming rather than merely inconvenient. The full set is on the prank screens index.
